name: PT MDS Retailing Tbk

frontmatter.title: MDS Retailing: a cash machine priced for a wind-down
frontmatter.summary: MDS Retailing runs Indonesia's largest department-store chain and still converts far more cash than its market value implies. The shares trade on 4.8x our FY2026E earnings and yield 16.7% because the market extrapolates structural decline. We see a smaller but durable estate, a gross margin that the mix keeps nudging higher and two non-operating assets the price gives away. Target Rp5,085; BUY.
thesis: The price discounts permanent decline: the reverse DCF needs revenue to fall -14.1% a year, while nine-month gross sales of IDR8,377.0bn were a low-single-digit decline and same-store sales were still positive over that period at 0.3%, though they slipped to -0.1% in the third quarter alone [S3].

Cash generation is the thesis, not growth: FY2025 free cash flow to the firm of IDR1,414.6bn against a market capitalisation of 4.8x our FY2026E earnings, and the FY2025 dividend cost IDR556.8bn [S0, S4].

Margins are cyclically depressed, not structurally broken: the direct-purchase mix rose to 34.4% of sales on a 41.5% DP margin against 31.6% on consignment, lifting nine-month gross margin to 35.2% [S3].
The dividend is credible: payout of 81.0% for FY2024, a dividend of Rp250 for FY2025 and 31.0m treasury shares retired in 2026 [S2, S4, S5].
Two assets the operating business does not need sit outside the DCF: investment property and quoted equity instruments of IDR195.5bn and IDR364.0bn [S4].
The bear case is worth Rp3,851 - the downside we can source is a slower recovery and a payout cut, not insolvency [S3, S0].

blocks.text: **BUY — target Rp5,085, 224.0% total return from Rp1,655.** MDS Retailing, until April 2026 PT Matahari Department Store, operates the largest department-store network in Indonesia: gross sales of IDR11,034.5bn in FY2025, a store estate spread across the archipelago and 7,521 employees [S2]. Gross sales are the company's own KPI and the basis on which this report states revenue and every revenue ratio; the audited income statement's top line is net revenue of IDR5,784.7bn for FY2025, lower because consignment sales enter the accounts net of the brand owner's share [S2]. The company books part of its business directly and part on consignment — retail sales through its own books were IDR3,357.4bn of merchandise sales in FY2025 against consignment sales of IDR7,694.6bn [S2] — and the direct-purchase share of the mix is the single most important margin lever we track [S3].

The market disagrees with us about duration, not about the near term. The shares trade on 4.8x our FY2026E earnings and 7.7x book, with a dividend yield of 16.7% [S0]. Our reverse DCF says those multiples are consistent only with revenue growth of -14.1% a year from FY2027E — a wind-down, not a retailer. Nine-month gross sales of IDR8,377.0bn were a low-single-digit decline, with same-store sales at 0.3% over the nine months but -0.1% in the third quarter alone, and gross margin up to 35.2% [S3]. We do not need a consumer recovery to justify the price; we need the estate to stop shrinking faster than the cash comes out, and the cash is already coming out.

Three drivers carry the call. First, cash generation against price: FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR1,414.6bn on gross sales of IDR11,034.5bn, and the FY2025 dividend of Rp250 a share cost IDR556.8bn [S0, S4]. After the lease principal that sits in financing, the cover is closer to one times than two — the cash flow is real, but it is committed to the estate as well as to the holder [S4]. Second, margin repair through mix: direct purchase reached 34.4% of sales, and gross margin rose to 35.2% in the nine months [S3]. Third, capital return and a cleaned-up register: the payout was 81.0% of FY2024 earnings against a 50.0% policy floor, and the 31.0m treasury shares held at the end of 2025 were retired in 2026, so per-share arithmetic finally matches the filings [S2, S4].

**On the firm macro tilt.** The house regime is balance-of-payments pressure and cautious, with rate-sensitive Indonesian consumer discretionary on avoid. Our base case is not a bet against that view: revenue falls -1.6% in FY2026E and a little further in FY2027E (-1.0%, the negative carry-over from the third quarter), well below CPI of 3.3%, so real volumes keep shrinking; gross margin is held near 34.9% and lifted only by the measured mix path, not recovered; capex stays at 1.7% of sales [S2, S3]. What we disagree with is the inference from a weak consumer to a business worth a fraction of its cash flow. If the cautious macro view proves right, the bear case at Rp3,851 is still above the price: the bear shocks growth and margin by the mirror image of the bull case, and adds a payout cut, rather than assuming a collapse.

**On the discarded idea card.** The sector file carried INDO-LPPF, marked DISCARD on 9 November 2026, on regime grounds — the same macro tilt above — and because it had no fundamentals anchor. We have answered the three questions it left open in this draft. Margins are cyclically rather than structurally depressed: nine-month gross margin rose on mix, and operating expenses fell year on year [S3]. The anchor gap is closed because the data pack is populated with four annual periods, seven quarters and an LTM [S0], and because the filings give us a complete share register, lease schedule and segment split [S2, S4]. The dividend is supported by cash flow rather than by leverage: free cash flow covered the FY2025 distribution and the company ended September with net cash before lease liabilities of IDR44.0bn [S3]. It is not wholly self-funding at the current pace — the April 2026 payment drew cash down from IDR448.3bn to IDR143.7bn and came with a new bank line of IDR100.0bn [S4] — but on a full-year basis operating cash flow after lease principal still covered what was paid in 2025 [S2]. We have therefore not let the discard dictate the view; we have let it set the burden of proof, and the evidence meets it.

**The share count needed correcting before any per-share work.** The data pack carries a share count roughly half the register; the filing shows issued and fully paid capital of 2,227.3m shares after the treasury retirement, and the share chronology runs from 2,260.3m in FY2023 to 2,258.3m at the end of FY2025, of which 31.0m were treasury and did not share in the dividend [S2, S4]. Every price ratio, per-share figure and target in this report uses the filing's count, and the engine's restatement is justified in the assumptions file. Two of the engine's display multiples do not: its EV/EBITDA and its free-cash-flow-to-equity yield are computed against the data pack's market capitalisation, which still carries the old count, so we quote neither and say why in the valuation section [S0, S4].

What would change our mind: a break in the dividend, a lease renewal cycle at materially higher rent than the IDR546.2bn of short-term and low-value rent charged in FY2025 [S2], or evidence that the direct-purchase mix is being bought with inventory risk rather than supplier terms.

Department stores everywhere have lost share to e-commerce, specialty chains and value formats, and
Indonesia is no exception: the format's economics depend on footfall in air-conditioned malls, a
supplier base willing to carry consignment inventory, and rental contracts that can be renegotiated
as leases expire. The recovery playbook is familiar — shrink the box count, push private label,
convert consignment to direct purchase where the margin is better, and return the cash that a
low-capex estate throws off rather than reinvesting it in new space.

MDS Retailing sells apparel, accessories, cosmetics and household goods through department stores and, increasingly, through smaller specialty formats. Gross sales were IDR11,034.5bn in FY2025, of which IDR3,357.4bn was retail sales booked by the stores themselves and IDR7,694.6bn consignment sales where the company acts as agent for brand owners [S2]. The consignment share matters for how the accounts read: on consignment the company earns a commission on the brand owner's stock without carrying the inventory, so the statutory income statement recognises only the commission, which is why the audited top line is net revenue of IDR5,784.7bn and the statutory gross margin — gross profit of IDR3,812.3bn over that net revenue — is roughly two thirds rather than the mid-thirties [S2, S4]. The mid-thirties margin the company reports is a gross-sales margin: the same rupiah of gross profit over the larger gross-sales denominator, and the number the deck uses for mix analysis [S3]. Both are right; they measure different things, and the balance-sheet inventory of IDR743.0bn is modest relative to gross sales because the consignment stock never enters it [S2, S3].

The operating model has three levers. The first is space: sales per square metre reached IDR1,191.8 thousand per square metre a month in FY2025, and the company opened 10 new stores in the year while closing seven underperforming stores, excluding conversions — the FY2025 accounts attribute part of the fall in lease liabilities to stores closed during the year [S2]. The second is mix: direct purchase, where the company buys and owns the stock, carries a better margin than consignment and reached 34.4% of sales by the third quarter of 2026, supported by private label and by exclusive third-party brands [S3]. The third is cost: operating expenses fell year on year in the nine months to September 2026, and short-term and low-value rent of IDR546.2bn runs through the operating line rather than through depreciation [S2, S3].

The format portfolio is being widened rather than replaced. Alongside the core MDS department stores, the company has launched SUKO, ZES and Mu+Ku — smaller, category-focused and value-oriented formats — with new openings at Pontianak and Surabaya in the third quarter and a plan to add specialty and multi-concept stores in East Java and Kalimantan in the fourth [S3]. Private label now spans apparel, footwear and household categories, and the company describes increasing private-label space in comparable stores as a margin initiative rather than a volume one [S3]. For a mature format, that is the right emphasis: the estate is not going to grow its way out of a weak consumer, so the return has to come from margin per square metre and from the cash the existing box generates.

Ownership and group structure are covered in the governance section, but two points belong here because they shape the business. First, control sits with Auric Digital Retail Pte Ltd at 43.1%, with PT Multipolar Tbk at 7.4% at 30 September 2026 and the remainder public [S4]. The Auric group became controlling shareholder in 2021 after acquiring a stake through Greater Universal Ltd in 2020, following a history that runs from the company's founding in 1958 through the Matahari Putra Prima listing, the 2009 transfer of the department-store division and the CVC Asia Fund III period [S6]. Second, the company renamed itself PT MDS Retailing Tbk at an extraordinary general meeting in April 2026, approved by an overwhelming majority of votes cast, while keeping the LPPF ticker [S5, S6].

Competitively the company is the incumbent scale player in mid-market department stores, but scale in this format is defensive rather than offensive: it buys better, negotiates mall rents better and can carry a private-label programme that smaller chains cannot, yet it has no pricing power against e-commerce or against value formats on a basket of basics [S2, S3]. We treat it as a mature cash-generative franchise with a shrinking addressable footprint, not as a growth retailer, and the forecasts reflect exactly that: revenue -1.6% in FY2026E and -1.0% in FY2027E, with a slow return to low single-digit growth thereafter as the new formats scale [S2, S3].

The demand backdrop is weak and getting no help from policy. Bank Indonesia's real retail sales index grew 0.6% year on year in September 2026, slower than the prior month, and the central bank projects 1.0% growth for October [S7]. The annual report sets out why: inflation was contained at 2.9%, but household purchasing power was squeezed by a 1.9% wage settlement, a rising share of informal employment and youth unemployment of 19.8% [S2]. The company's own deck adds the cost side — price increases from the mid-single digits to the mid-teens across household products in September 2026 versus the prior year — which is a demand tax on a mid-market customer [S3].

Against that, the department-store format is losing share within retail. We do not have a sourced market-share series for the format, and we will not invent one; what the data does show is that MDS's gross sales fell in the nine months while the retail index grew 0.6%, which is consistent with continued share loss to e-commerce and specialty formats [S3, S7]. The company's response — smaller formats, private label, direct purchase — is an attempt to compete on the categories where a physical store still wins: fit, touch, immediacy and price-led basics.

The five forces are unfavourable in the classic sense and stable in practice. Supplier power is moderate: brand owners need the shelf space, which is why consignment exists, but the best international brands can choose their channels and increasingly sell direct. Buyer power is high and rising, because the customer can price-compare instantly [S3]. New entrants are a real threat in the sense that e-commerce has near-zero marginal cost of reaching the same customer, but not in the sense of anyone building a competing department-store chain — the mall anchor format is not being replicated. Substitutes are abundant: specialty chains, value formats, marketplaces. Rivalry is intense but consolidated at the top, with MDS the largest chain and the smaller players competing on price.

Regulation cuts both ways. Consumer-protection and labelling rules raise the fixed cost of the direct-purchase model and of private label, and import policy affects the landed cost of the direct-purchase range, which is the margin engine; a weaker rupiah at Rp18,190/USD against the dollar raises that cost with a lag [S3]. On the other side, consumption support and the central bank's rate path — policy rate at 5.8%, real GDP growth of 5.3% in the house deck — set the ceiling on how much the consumer can recover. Our base case does not assume the ceiling is reached.

Where we differ from the cautious narrative is not about the industry direction but about the terminal state. A shrinking format with negative working capital, minimal capex and lease liabilities that amortise as stores close does not need growth to be valuable; it needs only that the decline is slower than the cash yield. The industry data — a retail index growing at 0.6%, a company losing a point or two of sales a year — is exactly the environment in which that arithmetic works [S7, S3].

Department-store retailing is a lease-heavy, working-capital-light business. The mall landlord
provides the box; the supplier, on consignment, provides much of the stock; the retailer provides the
brand, the operating discipline and the customer relationship. That structure means a mature chain can
run for years on very little capital expenditure, which is why the format has historically been a
dividend vehicle rather than a growth story, and why lease renewals — not new store openings — are the
event that decides its economics.

**Revenue.** Revenue in this report is gross sales, the company's own KPI; the audited top line is net revenue, which was IDR5,784.7bn in FY2025 against gross sales of IDR11,027.8bn because consignment enters the accounts at the commission only [S2]. On that gross-sales basis the top line has fallen for two consecutive years: IDR12,307.8bn in FY2024 and IDR11,034.5bn in FY2025, a decline of -10.3% as same-store sales fell 7.5% and the company closed stores [S2]. The nine months to September 2026 show the rate of decline easing — gross sales of IDR8,377.0bn, with net revenue of IDR4,550.8bn — but the exit rate does not: same-store sales were 0.3% for the nine months and -0.1% in the third quarter, with non-apparel down more than apparel was up [S3, S4]. Our FY2026E revenue of IDR10,858.0bn assumes the fourth quarter gives back part of the nine-month improvement, because the company itself flags price increases from the mid-single digits to the mid-teens on household goods and a consumer that trades down in the final quarter [S3]. We carry the third-quarter rate into FY2027E rather than the nine-month average, at IDR10,749.4bn, and growth returns only at 0.5% in FY2028E, still below inflation [S2, S3].

**Margins and costs.** The gross margin we model is the company's gross-sales margin: gross profit of IDR3,812.3bn over gross sales, 34.5% in FY2025 on an adjusted basis of 34.7% [S2]. The statutory margin on net revenue is a different number — the same gross profit of IDR3,812.3bn over net revenue of IDR5,784.7bn — and moves for the same reasons, so nothing in the mix analysis depends on which denominator we use [S2]. The margin reached 35.2% in the nine months as direct purchase climbed to 34.4% of sales [S3]. We hold 34.9% for FY2026E and lift it along the mix path thereafter: at the disclosed DP margin of 41.5% against 31.6% on consignment, a point of extra DP share is worth about a tenth of a point of margin, so a continued gain of roughly a point a year — a third of the gain achieved in the last year — is worth about a tenth of a point a year, reaching 35.1% by FY2030E [S3]. That is the lever the business section calls the most important, carried rather than frozen; it is still a smaller gain than the last year delivered. Operating expenses ran at 24.7% of revenue in the nine months after a year-on-year cut of several percent [S3], and we hold that ratio — no further operating leverage, and no reversal of the cost programme either. The result is EBIT of IDR1,107.5bn against IDR1,024.7bn, with an EBITDA margin of 16.5% versus 15.8% [S0].

**Below the line and leases.** Depreciation and amortisation of IDR684.1bn is dominated by right-of-use amortisation, which is why the D&A charge is large relative to capex [S4]. Interest expense of IDR240.8bn is mostly lease interest on liabilities of IDR2,170.0bn, with a single bank loan of IDR100.0bn [S3]. The effective tax rate is held at 19.0%, just above the IDR167.2bn actually paid on IDR892.6bn of pre-tax profit [S2].

**The fourth-quarter bridge.** FY2026E net profit of IDR770.0bn against the nine-month actual of IDR652.0bn [S3] implies a fourth quarter close to the prior-year quarter, and the difference is the net other gain rather than a weakening business. That line sits above operating profit in the accounts and below EBIT in our build, and the nine months have already booked IDR75.5bn of it — bazaar participation income, a reversal of closed-store and impairment provisions, a small loss on fixed-asset disposals and other gains [S4, note 20]. A nil full-year assumption would require a year-end charge equal and opposite to what has already been earned, and nothing in the third-quarter accounts discloses one, so FY2026E carries the nine-month actual as IDR75.5bn. From FY2027E the line is held at nil: FY2025's IDR103.4bn was not repeated in FY2024 or FY2023, which were negative (IDR-20.0bn and IDR-28.4bn), so there is no run-rate to extrapolate [S2]. The residual quarter is then a normal one: full-year revenue of IDR10,858.0bn less the nine-month IDR8,377.0bn, at the modelled gross margin, less the balance of the full-year interest charge of which the nine months absorbed IDR155.3bn [S4]. It is not a near-zero quarter, which is what the previous build implied. Because the line sits outside operating profit it does not enter FCFF: it raises earnings, the dividend and book value, and leaves the DCF unchanged.

**Cash flow and working capital.** Operating working capital is structurally negative at IDR-773.0bn, because consignment payables exceed inventory and receivables [S0, S2]. We hold it at -7.0% of revenue, which means working capital is close to neutral in the forecast and does not fund growth. Capex was IDR180.0bn in FY2025 and we hold 1.7% of revenue, enough for maintenance, selective renovation and the new formats, with store growth funded through leases rather than owned property [S2]. Free cash flow to the firm is IDR1,383.6bn, against the IDR556.8bn of dividend actually paid in the year and a forward distribution of 80.0% of FY2026E earnings, Rp277 a share [S0, S4]. We quote the cash paid rather than the engine's cash-flow line for the distribution because that line books each year's dividend on the prior year-end share count, and so still carries the 31m treasury shares retired in April 2026. The FY2026E payout is also struck on earnings that include the IDR75.5bn one-off, so the modelled Rp277 a share is above the Rp250 actually paid; applied to recurring earnings the same 80.0% payout would hold the distribution near the FY2025 level [S4].

That comparison is before the estate is paid for. Lease principal is a financing outflow — IDR541.4bn in the first nine months of 2026 — because the lease liability is treated as debt and deducted in the valuation, and it is not in FCFF [S4]. Deduct it and the nine-month cover falls well short of the distribution: operating cash flow of IDR795.6bn for the nine months less lease principal leaves under half of the IDR556.8bn of dividend paid in April 2026 [S4]. The gap was met from the balance sheet rather than from the year's trading: cash fell from IDR448.3bn at the end of 2025 to IDR143.7bn at September 2026, and the company carried a new bank borrowing of IDR100.0bn against none a year earlier [S4]. The full-year arithmetic is better than the nine-month one: FY2025 operating cash flow of IDR1,667.5bn less lease principal of IDR729.5bn still exceeded the IDR668.2bn of dividend actually paid during that year [S2]. The distribution is funded, but not wholly from the current year's cash generation, and the lease renewal cycle — not the margin — is what would break it.

**Balance sheet and debt.** The reported balance sheet is thin: equity of IDR272.9bn and book value per share of Rp121 at the end of FY2025, a legacy of buybacks and of a business that earns high returns on very little capital [S2]. It reconciles to the September 2026 accounts without a residual: equity of IDR360.0bn is the opening balance plus nine-month net profit of IDR652.0bn, less the IDR556.8bn dividend paid and the fair-value movement on the quoted equity portfolio [S4]. Debt of IDR2,569.9bn is almost entirely lease liabilities; excluding leases the company reported net cash of IDR44.0bn at September 2026, with IDR1,600.0bn of unused bank facilities, and inventory pledged against the working-capital line [S3, S2]. Our forecast net debt falls from IDR2,121.7bn to IDR830.2bn as leases run off and cash builds. The FY2026E step looks large — from lease liabilities of IDR2,170.0bn plus the IDR100.0bn bank line less IDR143.7bn of cash at September to IDR1,429.7bn at December — and it rests on a fourth quarter of operating cash of the order FY2025 delivered, the difference between the full-year IDR1,667.5bn and the nine-month IDR820.6bn [S2, S4]. The engine's cash line does not deduct lease principal, so the decline is a cash statement, not a claim that the estate has been repaid. The engine's balance sheet accumulates cash because the payout is set on accounting earnings while D&A exceeds capex; that is a modelling artefact of a high-payout retailer, not a forecast that the board will hoard cash, and the DCF values the business before that cash build.

**Capital allocation.** The company pays a large share of earnings: 81.0% of FY2024 net profit against a policy floor of 50.0% [S2], which was IDR668.2bn paid out during 2025 at Rp300 a share, and the FY2025 dividend of Rp250 a share cost IDR556.8bn, paid in 2026 on the shares in circulation [S4, S5]. It has also retired treasury stock: the buyback shares held at the end of 2024, 1.0m of them, were cancelled in April 2025, and the 31.0m held at the end of 2025 were cancelled in 2026, which is a cleaner use of capital than holding them [S2, S4]. With capex at 1.7% of sales, essentially all free cash flow is distributable — after the lease principal discussed above.

**Earnings quality.** We ran the house screens before committing estimates, and one of them stays open. Accruals are negative in the sense that matters: cash flow from operations of IDR795.6bn for the nine months exceeded net profit of IDR652.0bn [S4]. Inventory is the flag we cannot close. It was IDR954.8bn at the end of FY2025 against IDR727.5bn a year earlier, a build of about a third while gross sales fell -10.3%, and the December payables that funded it — IDR639.0bn of consignment and IDR668.0bn of direct-purchase trade payables — are visible on the deck's balance sheet [S2, S3]. At September the stock was IDR743.0bn against IDR739.0bn a year earlier — essentially flat, not worked down — so the year-end level was not run off: the divergence between inventory and sales is a genuine optics-class flag, not a screen we can close on a December-to-September comparison [S3]. It does not reach manipulation class — the stock is disclosed, ageing is discussed and there is no evidence of fictitious sales — but it caps how much of the mix gain we are willing to capitalise in the margin, which is why the mix path adds a tenth of a point a year rather than the full segment spread [S3]. There is no capitalised development cost and no sign of borrowing costs being parked on the balance sheet; the right-of-use asset of IDR1,569.0bn is disclosed and depreciated [S3, S4]. The auditor is KAP Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, a PricewaterhouseCoopers member firm, for a fee of IDR2.5bn with no non-audit services [S2]. Related-party dealings are disclosed in the notes and are not a visible channel of value leakage at the scale that would alter the earnings [S2]. The other data problem we found was the share count, which we restated rather than modelled around [S2, S4]. We classify no manipulation-class flag on this name; the structure flag is the controlled ownership, discussed in the governance section.

**Forecast summary.** By FY2028E the model has revenue of IDR10,803.1bn, EBITDA of IDR1,793.3bn and net profit of IDR750.9bn, with EPS of Rp337 and a dividend of Rp270 [S0]. Net profit dips in FY2027E before it recovers: that is the nine-month other gain of IDR75.5bn not carried forward, worth IDR728.6bn against IDR770.0bn on almost flat revenue, not an operating deterioration. The forecast is otherwise deliberately unheroic: it is the last actual year, re-priced at a flat benchmark, with the cost base held and no margin expansion beyond what the company has already delivered.

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with peer multiples as cross-checks. The choice follows the business: a mature, low-capex, high-payout retailer with negative working capital is better valued on the cash it distributes than on a near-term earnings multiple that embeds the market's view of its own decline. The weights are 60% DCF, 30% P/E and 10% EV/EBITDA, per the industry card [S0].

The cost of equity is 17.4%: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% embedded in the local-currency government yield, plus a levered beta of 1.72 on an equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. The unlevered beta of 0.90 is the industry default for a discretionary retailer. Cost of debt is 9.4% pre-tax, reflecting a book that is mostly lease liabilities, and the after-tax weighted cost of capital is 12.0% [S0]. One caveat, stated plainly: the engine measures leverage against the data pack's market capitalisation, which still carries the old share count, so the reported debt-to-equity of 1.17 and the beta built on it are too high. On the filing's count the market capitalisation is larger, gearing falls, the levered beta drops and the equity weight rises; the two effects very nearly cancel and re-levering on the filing's count lands the cost of capital a few basis points *below* the engine's figure — under five basis points, against a re-levered equity cost of roughly fourteen and three-quarters percent — so the shortcut is, if anything, fractionally conservative rather than flattering. We keep the engine's 12.0% and disclose it rather than hand-adjust, because a hand-adjustment would not be reproducible from the model.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR13,998.2bn and a value per share of Rp5,582, with the terminal value at 40.1% of the total [S0]. Terminal growth of 2.0% is below Indonesian inflation of 2.9% and far below nominal GDP growth, which is the right discipline for a format with flat volumes: we are not assuming the department store returns to growth, only that it stops shrinking. The forecast itself grows revenue at 0.5% by FY2028E and holds margins flat, so the value is coming from the conversion of EBIT into cash, not from an operating recovery.

Three discipline tests, as the compounder card requires. **Reinvestment.** Capex is 1.7% of sales against D&A of 6.3%, working capital is negative, so reinvestment is a small fraction of NOPAT: terminal growth of 2.0% needs only an incremental return of roughly the cost of capital, not an excess return. **Fade.** There is no fade schedule because there is almost nothing to fade — we capitalise no growth at excess returns. The margin held at 35.1% is below the last reported nine-month figure and the value comes from the existing asset base, which earns far more than its capital because the capital is tiny; a fade in returns on *new* capital would matter only if we were forecasting new capital, and capex below depreciation says we are not. **Multiple survival.** The terminal value, 40.1% of enterprise value, is struck on FY2035E EBITDA of IDR1,961.2bn against IDR1,791.6bn today. Set against the terminal year's earnings it implies an exit multiple a couple of percent above the entry multiple the DCF pays for today's EBITDA — close to flat, but not below it, and the whole of that premium comes from EBITDA being about a tenth higher in the terminal year, not from paying more for each rupiah of it. The honest version of the test is that the exit multiple is roughly double the peer-median EV/EBITDA of 4.3: our terminal value pays a multiple the market would only pay a retailer it expected to keep earning, which is the same disagreement as the cross-check below. The survival argument therefore rests on the terminal year's EBITDA being real, not on re-rating — and the value still clears the price on a terminal EBITDA halved.

The cross-checks disagree with the primary method, and the disagreement is the most important thing in this report. The peer-median P/E of 8.2 gives Rp2,858 a share, -48.8% versus the DCF; the peer-median EV/EBITDA of 4.3 gives Rp2,799, -49.9% below it [S0]. The peers are Indonesian listed retailers drawn from our own data packs, and their multiples are trailing, so they carry the de-rating that this whole report is about; a peer set is a mirror, not a second opinion. There are only two coherent explanations for the gap. The first is that the peer set is itself priced for decline — small, illiquid Indonesian retailers trade at trough multiples because the market applies the same discount to all of them — in which case the multiples are a statement about sentiment, not about value. The second is that our DCF is too generous, which would require the cash conversion to be an illusion; but the cash conversion is visible in the accounts, with cash flow from operations of IDR795.6bn in nine months against a IDR556.8bn annual dividend and capex at 1.7% of sales [S4, S2]. We weight the DCF at 60% precisely because we believe the first explanation, and we flag the gap rather than smoothing it: if a reader believes the peer multiples, the shares are worth around Rp2,799 and the stock is still not expensive at Rp1,655.

**Two display artefacts, disclosed rather than used.** The engine's forward EV/EBITDA and its free-cash-flow-to-equity yield are computed against the data pack's market capitalisation, IDR1,936.7bn, which is the stale share count times the price rather than the filing's 2,227.3m shares; the same figure sets the debt-to-equity in the cost of capital above. On the filing's count the market capitalisation is larger and both yields are correspondingly lower. We therefore quote neither ratio anywhere in this report — the P/E, P/BV and dividend yield are on the filing's count and are the multiples we use — and we point the reader to the enterprise value and net debt in the DCF table instead, where the arithmetic is on the corrected share count [S0, S4].

**What the operating business does not own.** The DCF values the retail cash flows and then deducts net debt; it does not see two assets that sit on the same balance sheet. At 30 September 2026 the company held investment property of IDR195.5bn at fair value and IDR364.0bn of quoted equity instruments — a listed stake in Nobu Bank marked to market — and neither produces the retail cash flow we forecast [S4]. We add both to the valuation bridge at full value: together they exceed the dividend the company paid for FY2025, and leaving them out would understate the company by more than the whole of its last distribution. Nothing about them is encumbered: the property is carried at appraised fair value and the shares are listed and marked at the closing price [S4].

The sensitivity table spans the two drivers that matter: terminal growth and the cost of capital. A percentage-point move in WACC is worth roughly a fifth of the value per share, and a percentage-point move in terminal growth slightly less; the conclusion — that the shares are worth several times the price unless the business is terminal — survives either. The second grid spans revenue growth and gross margin, which is where a higher lease renewal lands: renewal rent sits in the operating line, not in capex, so a mall that re-prices a store is a gross-margin event and the grid's margin axis is its sensitivity. The size of that risk is measurable: short-term and low-value rent of IDR546.2bn is about a twentieth of gross sales of IDR11,027.8bn, so a renewal cycle that repriced a tenth of the estate upwards would cost roughly half a point of gross margin — inside the grid's margin axis, which spans a point either way — and a sharper re-pricing of the whole estate is a shock the bear case does not need in order to reach its target. The scenario table below applies the same discipline to the operating drivers.

**What the price implies.** We reverse-engineered the current price. At Rp1,655 the market is discounting revenue growth of -14.1% a year from FY2027E on our margin and cost structure [S0]. For that to be right, the estate would have to shrink faster than the leases run off, which is the opposite of what the nine months show: gross margin up, operating costs down, and same-store sales at 0.3% over the period [S3]. It is not the opposite of what the latest quarter shows: same-store sales were -0.1% in the third quarter, so the market's extrapolation and the company's exit rate are closer than the year-to-date figure suggests. We do not claim the market is irrational; we claim it is extrapolating a decline that is slowing, not one that has stopped.

**Post-balance-sheet review.** We searched for events after the 30 September 2026 balance sheet that would change the value: the third-quarter statements and deck, the April 2026 name change, and the dividend declaration. There is no divestment, no special distribution declared since the FY2025 payout, no rights issue, and the treasury retirement is already in the share count [S3, S4, S5]. What the review did find is the two non-operating assets added to the bridge above, and an equity reconciliation that needs stating: the company's equity of IDR360.0bn at 30 September 2026 is the FY2025 closing balance plus comprehensive profit for the nine months, less the IDR556.8bn dividend paid, with the treasury retirement moving value between equity lines and not out of equity [S4]. The model's opening equity is the audited FY2025 close, so the DCF starts from the same balance sheet the bridge is measured against.

The market's reluctance to pay for a declining retailer is rational: terminal-value models are
extremely sensitive to the assumed end state, and a department store that loses a tenth of its sales
a year is worth very little however cheap it looks on current earnings. The counter-argument is not
that decline will stop, but that the decline is already in the price several times over, and that the
cash distributed along the way is worth more than the equity market is paying for the whole business.

**Consumer and macro (high likelihood, high impact).** This is the live risk. Retail sales growth of 0.6% and a central bank forecast of 1.0% describe a consumer that is not recovering [S7]; if the fourth quarter is weaker than the company's own commentary implies, revenue could fall faster than our -1.6% [S3]. The bear case cuts revenue growth by three points, takes a point and a half off gross margin and cuts the payout well below the 80.0% base — towards, though the engine's scenario bound will not let it reach, the 50.0% policy floor. It produces Rp3,851, which is still above the price, and that is the honest statement of the case: on the shocks we can source, the shares remain worth more than they cost. The bear is an enterprise-value case. The scenario that gets the shares to Rp1,655 is the one the market is already discounting — revenue falling at the reverse-DCF rate for a decade — and we do not accept it as the most likely path, but we cannot rule it out, which is why the bear is the case to watch rather than a floor.

**Margin and mix (medium likelihood, high impact).** The direct-purchase model carries inventory risk that consignment does not. If the mix shift stalls or if inventory has to be marked down, gross margin gives back the gain. The inventory line is the evidence, and it cuts against us: stock built by about a third in FY2025 while sales fell, and at September it was IDR743.0bn against IDR739.0bn a year earlier, flat rather than worked down [S2, S3]. That is a markdown waiting to happen, not a buffer.

**Input costs and currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Direct purchase is dollar-denominated at the margin, and the house deck depreciates the rupiah from Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E to Rp18,850/USD by FY2029E [S0]. A weaker rupiah raises landed cost with a one-to-two quarter lag, and the company's own commentary on price increases in household goods shows that suppliers are already passing costs through [S3].

**Leases and the estate (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Rent of IDR546.2bn for short-term and low-value leases runs through operating costs, and the lease liability of IDR2,170.0bn at September 2026 was lower than at the start of the year as stores closed [S2, S3]. The cash cost is not small: lease principal was IDR541.4bn in the first nine months of 2026, against operating cash flow of IDR795.6bn and a dividend of about IDR556.8bn [S4]. The risk is a renewal cycle at higher occupancy cost in the malls where the company must stay, which would compress the margin without showing up in the DCF's capex line — the sensitivity grid's margin axis is where it lands.

**Governance and control (low likelihood, high impact).** A controlling shareholder at 43.1% can decide the dividend, related-party terms and the pace of store closures [S4]. The dividend record is strong and the payout policy explicit, but a controlling holder with a different liquidity need is the structural risk on any high-yield IDX small cap — and the second-largest holder has been reducing, which we discuss in the governance section [S2, S4].

**Liquidity (medium likelihood, low impact for us).** Average daily traded value is IDR2.9bn, about a tenth of a percent of the market capitalisation, with no zero-volume sessions in the pack [S0]. Sizing against it: a tenth of daily turnover is a few hundred million rupiah a day, so a position worth one percent of the register would take about half a year to accumulate at that participation and cannot be exited quickly under stress. The free float is 47.5% of the register, which matches the filing's public and treasury line and contradicts the pack's insider field of 78.3%. We cannot reconcile the two and say so: the filing's register adds the controllers to 43.1% and 7.4% and leaves the remainder public, which is the free-float figure we use, while the pack's insider field implies a third block nobody has disclosed [S4]. We therefore use the filing's register and treat the pack field as stale and unexplained rather than let it size the float. The engine's zero liquidity discount is defensible for a patient holder at that size but not for an exit under stress, and we would not underwrite a position larger than a tenth of daily turnover [S0].

**Signposts that would change the view.** A dividend cut or a payout below the policy floor; same-store sales negative on the third quarter's exit rate for two consecutive quarters; a gross-margin reversal below the FY2025 level; a lease renewal disclosed at materially higher cost; or a related-party transaction that moves cash away from minority holders [S2, S3, S4].

Retail turnarounds fail more often than they succeed, and the failure mode is usually the same: the
company cuts costs and closes stores, the customer notices, and the sales decline accelerates past the
cost savings. The reason this case is not that story is the balance sheet — negative working capital,
minimal capex and lease liabilities that shrink with the estate mean the cash comes out before the
decline is fully visible. That is also why the bear case is bounded: the company can shrink into
profitability for longer than a leveraged retailer could.

**Ownership and control.** At 30 September 2026 Auric Digital Retail Pte Ltd holds 43.1% and PT Multipolar Tbk 7.4%, with public shareholders at the balance of the 2,227.3m shares in issue [S4]. The register has moved in two ways this year. Auric's percentage rose without buying a share, because the 31.0m treasury shares were cancelled in April 2026 and the denominator fell; and Multipolar's holding fell from 210.0m shares at the 2025 annual report date to 164.8m at 30 September 2026, a reduction of more than a fifth of its position and a meaningful slice of the free float. That is a signal worth respecting in a stock whose thesis rests on the controller's appetite for distributing cash [S2, S4]. Auric became controlling shareholder in 2021 after acquiring a stake through Greater Universal Ltd in 2020, following the CVC Asia Fund III period and, before that, the Matahari Putra Prima listing [S6]. There is no disclosed pledge of the controlling shareholder's shares in the annual report, and we checked [S2]. The treasury overhang is gone: 1.0m shares held at the end of 2024 were cancelled in April 2025 and the 31.0m held at the end of 2025 were cancelled in 2026, so the register is now one class of shares with no treasury [S2, S4].

**Board and auditor.** The board includes an independent commissioner, and the annual report carries the standard responsibility statement signed by the board [S2]. The auditor is KAP Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, a PricewaterhouseCoopers member firm, for a fee of IDR2.5bn with no non-audit services in 2025 [S2]. The FY2025 accounts were audited without qualification in our reading of the opinion, and the company has not changed auditor tier in the period we cover [S2].

**Related parties and minority protection.** The notes disclose the nature of related-party relationships and transactions annually [S2]; in the period we cover there is no single transaction large enough to distort the earnings, and no cash advance to affiliates of the scale that would be a red flag. Inventory is pledged against the working-capital facility [S2], which is a lender protection, not a minority one. The main structural point is simply that a controlled company with a high payout is only as good as the controller's appetite for distributing cash — and on the record so far, that appetite is strong: 81.0% of FY2024 profit and a FY2025 dividend of Rp250 that cost IDR556.8bn [S2, S5].

**Dividend record.** Dividends per share were Rp200, Rp300 and Rp250 in the last three fiscal years [S0, S2]. The FY2025 payout was IDR556.8bn on net profit of IDR725.4bn [S4, S2]: a ratio of just over three-quarters, measured on the 2,227.3m shares entitled to it after the April 2026 retirement rather than on the 2,258.3m issued shares that still carried the treasury block, which is the trap in the pre-retirement denominator. We hold the forecast at 80.0%, above the actual and below the FY2024 print of 81.0%, because the rupiah dividend per share is struck once a year on a falling share count. The distinction that matters here is declared against paid: the payout declared against FY2023 earnings was 67.0% of that year's profit, above the policy floor but below earnings, while the cash dividend actually paid during FY2023 — IDR1,186.1bn, the distribution declared against FY2022 — exceeded that year's net profit of IDR675.4bn [S0, S2]. The appetite to distribute beyond a single year's earnings is real; it is the timing of the cash, not the payout ratio, that is easy to misread.

**ESG.** The material exposures are social and supply chain: a workforce of 7,521, a direct-purchase programme that sources from Asian manufacturers, and a private-label supply chain where labour standards are the main risk [S2]. Energy use in air-conditioned stores is the main environmental exposure, and the company reports on it in the annual report's sustainability section [S2]. We do not score the company highly on disclosure depth — it is a standard IDX sustainability report rather than a best-in-class one — but we see no exposure that would change the investment case.

Governance on the Indonesian exchange is where value is most often destroyed, and the modal channel
is related-party dealings between a controlled listed company and the controller's private
businesses. The screens that matter are therefore the ones this report has run: who controls the
company, whether the controller's shares are pledged, whether the auditor is a credible firm, whether
the dividend is actually paid in cash, and whether related-party flows are disclosed and quantified.

**Near-dated catalysts.** The Bank Indonesia October retail sales survey, due within days of this note, is projected to show a return to growth of 1.0% after September's 0.6% [S7]. The company plans new specialty and multi-concept openings in East Java and Kalimantan in the fourth quarter, which will be the first read on whether the new formats travel beyond Java [S3]. The FY2026 audited results and the dividend proposal follow the annual cycle in the first quarter of 2027, with the annual general meeting in April on the 2026 calendar [S2, S6].

**What we monitor between updates.** Same-store sales and the direct-purchase share, both disclosed quarterly; gross margin, which is the cleanest read on mix and on input costs; operating expenses, where the cost programme has to keep pace with falling sales; inventory, as the leading indicator of markdown risk; the lease liability balance, which tells us how fast the estate is shrinking; and the dividend, which is the return the thesis actually delivers [S2, S3].

**What would make us wrong.** A break in the dividend or a payout below the policy floor would invalidate the cash-return leg of the thesis. Two consecutive quarters of negative same-store sales would suggest the third-quarter stabilisation was a base effect. A gross-margin reversal below the FY2025 level would say the mix shift is being bought, not earned. Any of those would move us toward the bear case rather than the target [S2, S3].

bear.narrative: Consumer spending stays weak, SSSG turns negative again and the department-store format keeps losing share to e-commerce and specialty formats; gross margin gives back the 2026 gain as input costs stay high and price rises meet resistance, while rents renew higher. Capital return breaks with it: the board cuts the payout to the 50% policy floor as lease principal and a weaker cash flow squeeze the distribution.

bull.narrative: The 2026 stabilisation holds and the SUKO, ZES and MU+KU formats scale faster, lifting SSSG and the direct-purchase mix; gross margin keeps improving and the cost programme sticks, so the cash payout is sustained on a rising earnings base and the board tops it up towards the limit of what free cash flow after lease principal can carry.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -1.6% is the nine-month actual (gross sales 8,377 vs 8,512, S3) with a soft Q4 on input-cost-led price rises and falling consumer confidence; FY2027E -1.0% carries the third quarter's exit rate (3Q26 gross sales -1.9% yoy and SSSG -0.1%, versus +0.3% for the nine months, S3) rather than assuming the nine-month average is the run-rate; the path then lifts to +1.2% by FY2029E as the SUKO/ZES/MU+KU formats scale, still below CPI of 3.3% (macro deck), i.e. real volume decline for a mature department-store format.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M26 gross margin was 35.2% on the gross-sales basis, up 0.5pp year on year on a higher direct-purchase mix (34.4% of sales vs 31.2%, S3) and private-label space; we hold 34.9% for FY2026E (Q4 absorbs cotton +16% and PTA +30% input inflation reported in S3). Thereafter we carry the mix lever rather than freeze it: at the disclosed segment margins of 41.5% for DP and 31.6% for consignment (S3), each point of extra DP share is worth about a tenth of a point of gross margin, so a continued gain of roughly a point a year - a third of the 3.2pp gained in the last year - adds 0.1pp a year to 35.1% by FY2030E, still below the 9M26 print.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M26 operating expenses fell 3.9% year on year (S3) and equal 24.7% of revenue; we hold that ratio, i.e. no operating leverage beyond the cost programme already delivered, with rent for short-term and low-value leases (Rp546.2bn in FY2025, S2) inside the line.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A of Rp723.7bn (total depreciation Rp689.5bn plus amortisation Rp34.2bn, S2/S4) was 6.6% of revenue and 9M26 depreciation was Rp508.4bn (S4); held at 6.3% because the charge is dominated by right-of-use amortisation (Rp376.7bn in 9M26, S4). The gap to capex (1.7% of revenue) is therefore almost entirely non-cash lease amortisation against lease principal of Rp541.4bn paid in 9M26 (S4, fact F56), which sits in financing because the lease liability is treated as debt and deducted from enterprise value; renewals are assumed at the existing rent already inside the operating line (Rp546.2bn of short-term and low-value rent, S2) with the new right-of-use asset matched by a new liability, so no renewal capex is added.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash capex was Rp180bn (S2) or 1.6% of revenue, and total additions of fixed assets and right-of-use assets were Rp199.2bn (S2); we hold 1.7% of revenue, enough for maintenance, selective renovations and the new mono-brand formats, with store growth funded through leases.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital is structural: payables from concession and direct-purchase suppliers exceed inventory and receivables (FY2025 net working capital -Rp773.0bn, S0), held at -7.0% of revenue, the FY2025 level.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 18.7% of pre-tax profit (Rp167.2bn on Rp892.6bn, S2); held at 19.0%, just above the last actual and below the 22% statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Three-year average of interest expense over opening debt is 9.4%; the debt is mostly lease liabilities (Rp2,170bn of Rp2,270bn at September 2026, S3) so the implied rate is a blend of lease interest and the Rp100bn bank loan.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Three-year average of interest income over opening cash (S0); cash is small and seasonal.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E repays Rp300bn as the right-of-use book runs down to the September 2026 balance sheet (debt Rp2,269.6bn, S3); debt is held flat afterwards as expiring leases are renewed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The nine months to September 2026 already booked a Rp75.5bn net other gain (F70, S4 note 20: bazaar participation Rp50.5bn, reversal of impairment and closed-store provisions Rp2.1bn, loss on fixed-asset disposal Rp4.5bn, other gains Rp27.3bn), so a nil FY2026E would require a year-end charge equal and opposite to what the accounts have already earned; nothing in the 3Q26 LK discloses one. We carry the nine-month actual for FY2026E and hold nil from FY2027E because the line has no run-rate to extrapolate: FY2025 was Rp103.4bn but FY2024 and FY2023 were losses of Rp20.0bn and Rp28.4bn (S2 p.10). This line sits below EBIT in our build (above operating profit in the LK), so it lifts earnings, the dividend and book value but is outside FCFF and does not change the DCF.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interests in the consolidated accounts (S2); held at zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The policy is a minimum 50% of net income (F23, S2) and the board has paid 81% for FY2024 (F24, S2) and 76.8% for FY2025 — Rp556.82bn of dividend (F5, S4 p.8) on Rp725.38bn of net profit (F3, S2), i.e. Rp250 per share (F4) on the 2,227,279,280 shares entitled after the April 2026 retirement, which is why the ratio is below the 78% a pre-retirement denominator would give. We hold 80%, 3.2pp above that actual and 1pp below the FY2024 print: earnings rise in FY2026E on a lower share count while the rupiah dividend per share is struck once a year, so the ratio drifts up mechanically, and the board has shown it will pay above the 50% floor when cash allows. The distribution is covered by free cash flow.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 2,258,279,280 shares were in issue at 31 December 2025 (F7, S4 p.6) and 2,227,279,280 at 30 September 2026, the difference being the 31.0m treasury shares retired in April 2026 (F6, F30, S4 p.6). The change therefore happens inside FY2026E, not at the boundary: FY2026E carries -1.373% (31.0m / 2,258.279m) and every later year is held flat, so the engine's forecast share line drops to the filing's 2,227.279m from FY2026E onwards and EPS, DPS, BVPS and dividends_paid all use the post-retirement count. No new buyback is announced, so the change is zero after that year.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0% nominal, below Indonesian CPI of 3.3% in the house macro deck and far below nominal GDP, reflecting a mature department-store format with flat volumes; above the 1.2% explicit FY2030E path because the store base stabilises rather than keeps shrinking.

challenges.challenge: The summary's 1.9x EV/EBITDA is the engine's display multiple, computed as (mcap_rep 1,936.7 + FY2026E net debt 1,490.8) / EBITDA 1,791.6 - and mcap_rep is 1,170.2m shares times Rp1,655, the very stale count the report says it has corrected. On the filing's 2,227.3m shares the same measure is 2.89x, or 3.32x on spot net debt. The same mcap_rep sets the WACC's D/E of 1.17, so the claim that every multiple uses the filing's count is false for the one multiple in the first paragraph.
challenges.answer: Both engine ratios are now labelled market-cap-stale and withheld from the report; the P/E, P/BV and dividend yield are on the filing's 2,227.3m shares. Re-levering at that count gives D/E of 0.62, a levered beta of 1.33 and a cost of capital a few basis points below the engine's figure (under five), i.e. fractionally conservative rather than flattering; the 12.1% in the challenge is not what the arithmetic gives [S4].

challenges.challenge: The compounder card makes the fade schedule and the multiple-survival test mandatory. Neither appears: there is no implied exit multiple from the Rp15,693bn terminal value, no reinvestment rate or ROIIC, no fade year, and the model holds a 10.2% EBIT margin for ten years with 2% terminal growth for a format sections 1 and 2 say is losing share to e-commerce and specialty chains.
challenges.answer: Added the reinvestment bridge (capex 1.7% of sales against D&A of 6.3% and negative working capital, so growth needs almost no new capital), the reason no fade schedule is warranted (no growth capitalised at excess returns; margins held below the last nine-month print), and the multiple-survival test: the exit multiple on FY2035E EBITDA is a couple of percent above the entry multiple, roughly double the peer median, so survival rests on terminal EBITDA being real, not on re-rating [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Every revenue figure in the report is gross sales, not the audited top line. Model FY2025A revenue of 11,034.5 matches S2 p.72 Gross Sales of 11,027.8, while the same table gives Net Revenue of 5,784.7; S4 p.7 shows 9M26 net revenue of 4,550.8 against the 8,377 the report calls gross sales, and the statutory gross margin is 64.6% in 9M26 and 65.9% in FY2025, not the 34.5-35.2% the report calls the reported margin. Section 1's explanation that consignment is why the reported gross margin is high is therefore inverted, and a reader cannot tie the report to the LK without the gross/net distinction.
challenges.answer: The basis is now stated wherever revenue appears: gross sales is the company KPI and the basis of every revenue ratio, and the audited net revenue line is quoted beside it for FY2025 and 9M26. Section 1 now explains the mechanics correctly: consignment books only a commission, so net revenue is smaller and the statutory gross margin is about two thirds, while the mid-thirties margin is gross profit over gross sales and is the one the deck uses for mix [S2, S4].

challenges.challenge: Dividend arithmetic contradicts its own citation: the summary and section 3 both say a Rp250 dividend cost IDR668.2bn. At the report's own 2,227.3m shares that is 556.8bn, which is exactly S4's 556,820; the 668.2 is the FY2024 distribution (S2 p.85, Rp668.2bn, DPS 300, 81% payout). The model inherits the error because dividends_paid uses dps[-1], so FY2025A pays FY2024's dividend. The same paragraph also says the treasury block held at the end of 2024 was retired in 2026, but the 31.0m cancelled in 2026 was the block held at end-2025 (F30 is labelled FY2024A; the 2024 block was 1,013,600, retired in 2025).
challenges.answer: FY2025 distribution corrected to Rp556.8bn (DPS 250 on 2,227.3m shares) and the payout to 78%; the Rp668.2bn figure is the FY2024 payout (DPS 300, 81%) paid during 2025 and now carries its own facts. F30 is relabelled to the end-2025 block retired in April 2026, the 1.01m block cancelled in April 2025 is separate, and dividend coverage is restated after lease principal [S2, S4].

challenges.challenge: The stabilisation claims rest on the cumulative figure. S3 p.6 reads '+0.3% YTD Same-store Sales Growth (SSSG), (Q3: -0.1%)' and p.10 says SSSG declined 0.1%, with non-apparel -6.6% and outside-Java -2.1% offsetting apparel +3.9%. The report says same-store sales are positive at 0.3% and that the last three quarters show same-store sales positive, so the reverse-DCF rebuttal that the market is extrapolating a decline that has stopped is materially weaker than stated.
challenges.answer: The Q3 exit rate of -0.1% is now quoted beside the +0.3% nine-month figure in the summary, section 1, section 3 and the reverse DCF; the base case carries FY2027E revenue of -1.0% precisely as the negative carry-over rather than assuming the nine-month average is the run-rate; the bear narrative and the section 7 signposts include the Q3 deterioration [S3].

challenges.challenge: Inventory is misread against the deck. Section 3 says it fell to 743 from the prior year's level and section 5 says 743 at September against a higher level a year earlier is a reduction. S3 states Sep-26 743 against Sep-25 739, up 0.5% vs LY - a build, not a reduction - and the pack shows FY2025 year-end inventory of 954.8 against 727.5, a 31% build while revenue fell 10.3%, which is exactly the divergence the house earnings-quality card flags. Using Dec-25 as the comparison closes a screen the accounts open.
